scenes.title: DENSE_RANK()
scenes.narration: DENSE_RANK ranks rows within a partition where ties share a rank but the next rank is always consecutive, leaving no gaps.

scenes.title: How DENSE_RANK() Behaves
bullets: Orders rows by the ORDER BY inside OVER
Tied rows share the same rank
The next rank increments by exactly one (1, 1, 2)
scenes.narration: DENSE_RANK orders rows and assigns positions much like RANK. Tied rows share the same rank. The difference is that the next distinct value always increases by exactly one, producing sequences like one, one, two with no gaps. Ranking still resets for each partition.

scenes.title: RANK() vs DENSE_RANK()

left.title: RANK()
points: Good for standings where gaps matter

right.title: DENSE_RANK()
points: Good for distinct tiers or levels

scenes.narration: Both functions let ties share a rank, so the split is entirely about what comes next. RANK skips positions, giving one, one, three, which leaves gaps that reflect how many rows tied. DENSE_RANK never skips, giving one, one, two, so the numbers stay compact. Use RANK when gaps are meaningful and DENSE_RANK when you want clean, consecutive tiers.

scenes.title: Salary Tiers Per Department
scenes.code:
SELECT
  department,
  employee_name,
  salary,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC
  ) AS salary_tier
FROM employees;
scenes.narration: Here we assign a salary tier within each department. Because we partition by department, the tiers reset for every group. DENSE_RANK ensures the tier numbers are consecutive, so if two employees share the top salary they are both tier one and the next-highest salary is tier two. This gives you clean, gap-free bands that are ideal for grouping employees into distinct pay levels.

scenes.text: Reach for DENSE_RANK() when you want the Nth distinct value — like the 3rd-highest salary — since it counts unique values without leaving gaps.
scenes.narration: DENSE_RANK is the right choice when you need the Nth distinct value, such as the third-highest salary, because it counts unique values without skipping.
